summary: A discussion of how people can write down X.400 originator/recipient (O/R) names in a uniform, human-friendly way. X.400 is the OSI email system, and its addresses are made of several named parts. This informational memo proposes a common way to write them.

plainLanguage.summary: Mail addresses in one old email system had many pieces. This note suggests one tidy way to write them so everyone spells them the same.

questions: what is an x.400 o/r name
what do g s o p a c mean in x.400
subtitle: A uniform way for people to write down the many-part addresses used by X.400 email.

tldr.problem: X.400 mail addresses (O/R names) are made of several named parts, and people had no single agreed way to write them on paper or type them in.
tldr.mechanism: RARE recommends following the ITU/ISO labelled format: short labels such as G, S, O and C joined to values with '=', separated by semicolons, in a fixed order.
tldr.outcome: The memo is informational and carries a copy of the draft standard annex that defines the format, so business cards and mail programs can all spell addresses the same way.

today: RFC 1685 is an Informational RFC from August 1994 and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It also says that for authoritative text the ITU standard itself should be consulted, since the annex it contains is a copy of a draft.

sections.title: Why a Uniform Notation Is Needed
sections.content:
People who use X.400 messaging systems need to be able to write down O/R names (originator/recipient names) in a uniform way. RARE already had a recommendation for this. Once the ISO/ITU adopted its own recommendation, RARE needed to update its advice to take that standard into account.

The memo is informational and does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old email addresses had lots of parts. This note says everybody should write those parts the same way so nobody gets confused.

sections.title: RARE's Recommendations
sections.content:
RARE recommends following the ISO standard. Because that standard has many options, RARE picks these:

  • Use the main abbreviations G, I, S, O, OU1, OU2, P, A and C, written in upper case.
  • Use a semicolon (;) as the separator.
  • A blank ADMD value is written by omitting the attribute. No other interpretation of a missing ADMD attribute is allowed.
  • Use the sequence G=;I=;S=;O=;OU1=;OU2=;P=;A=;C=;

This puts O, OU1 and so on in the opposite order to the fields of an Internet domain name. The ISO/ITU order was chosen because it will be more common among users of X.400 services.
sections.plainLanguage: Pick one kind of separator, use capital letters for the labels, and always list the pieces in the same order. That way a card from one person works in anyone's mail program.

sections.title: The Labelled Format
sections.content:
Section 3 copies a draft of the relevant ITU/ISO annex (Annex F). It describes a labelled format made of label=value pairs. Labels may be upper or lower case, but upper case is recommended because it is more visually distinctive.

Pairs in a sequence are separated by ; or /, but only one of these can be used in one address. With /, the first label is also prefixed by /. If a value contains the delimiter, the delimiter is doubled. If an identifier is needed in front of the address, X.400 is recommended.

The labels include G (given name), I (initials), S (surname), Q (generation qualifier), CN (common name), O, OU1 to OU4, P (PRMD), A (ADMD) and C (country). Further tables give labels for physical delivery attributes and other attributes, including DDA:<type> for domain defined attributes.

The annex also describes a self-explanatory format for places with more room, where each attribute name, in any language, is followed by its label.
sections.plainLanguage: Each piece gets a short tag, like G for given name and C for country, then an equals sign and the value. Pieces are split with semicolons, like commas in a list.

sections.title: Examples and User Interfaces
sections.content:
The annex's example is G=john; S=smith; O=a bank ltd; P=abl; A=snomail; C=aq. The same data can be laid out as a table, or written in a self-explanatory form using Norwegian attribute names followed by the labels, such as Fornavn (G).

For user interfaces, the annex says a command line must accept any valid labelled address with either delimiter, in any attribute order and in upper or lower case. If a user gives a PRMD but omits the ADMD, or gives it no value, the ADMD used is a single space. Form-fill interfaces must let users easily match each field to its label.
sections.plainLanguage: If you get a business card with the short tags, you can type it straight into the computer. If the card is in another language, the tags in brackets tell you which box each piece goes in.
